title: Whose Ditch
passage:
Until 1845 the hedge had never been in dispute. It was a thorn bank over a ditch between two Huntingdonshire farms, cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other, and had stood since the enclosure. An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane. In November 1845 Ephraim Ruddiforth’s attorney claimed the bank, the ditch and the timber from the stone gap down to the lane. The letters run to March; both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839. The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan. The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line along the bank, from the ash to the culvert. In February Ruddiforth offered to leave the timber and keep the ground. The scheme was given up in the autumn of 1846; no land was taken. In 1851 both farms laid the thorn together.
– Nigel Garner

questions.rationale:
The answer is D, and the passage never puts the two halves of it in one sentence. One half is the reach of the claim: in November 1845 Ruddiforth’s attorney asked for the bank, the ditch and the timber “from the stone gap down to the lane”. The other is the surveyor’s work of the month before, when the line was chained and pegged “along the bank, from the ash to the culvert”. Those are two different pairs of landmarks, and nothing ties them together until you go back to the description of the ground: “An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane.” Put the three sentences side by side and the pegged line and the claimed strip begin and end at the same two places. What Ruddiforth did in February shows what that strip had come to be worth: given the choice, he let the timber go and held on to the ground, which is a strange bargain for a man who wants a hedge. D asserts the overlap and stops there; it makes no claim about compensation, which never fell due.

C is the likeliest place to go wrong, because the survey is reported after the letters and the order of the telling is not the order of the events. The pegging is dated “The previous October”, the claim is dated “November 1845”, and the pegs were therefore in the ground before the first letter was written. A is a denial rather than a detail, and it slips past a hurried reader because Ruddiforth’s side does all the claiming and the neighbour’s side seems only to answer; but the sentence that records the answer is “The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan”, so it was the neighbour’s side that brought the railway into the letters. Neither attorney is named anywhere in the passage, and the only thing to go on is which side each of them acts for. B offers the ordinary occasion of a boundary quarrel, a hedge nobody has kept, and two sentences remove it: the bank was “cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other” and had “stood since the enclosure”, and the sentence that dates the thorn adds “both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839”, six years before the first letter and an unremarkable point in a laying cycle. Each wrong answer collides with a sentence instead of merely reaching past one.

The answer is D, and the passage never puts the two halves of it in one sentence. One half is the reach of the claim: in November 1845 Ruddiforth’s attorney asked for the bank, the ditch and the timber “from the stone gap down to the lane”. The other is the surveyor’s work of the month before, when the line was chained and pegged “along the bank, from the ash to the culvert”. Those are two different pairs of landmarks, and nothing ties them together until you go back to the description of the ground: “An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane”. Put the three sentences side by side and the pegged line and the claimed strip begin and end at the same two places. What Ruddiforth did in February shows what that strip had come to be worth: given the choice, he let the timber go and held on to the ground, which is a strange bargain for a man who wants a hedge. D asserts the overlap and stops there; it makes no claim about compensation, which never fell due.

C is the likeliest place to go wrong, because the survey is reported after the letters and the order of the telling is not the order of the events. The pegging is dated “The previous October”, the claim is of “November 1845”, and the pegs were therefore in the ground before the first letter was written. A is a true detail with the two sides exchanged, and it survives a hurried reading because the tracing really is in the file; but the sentence that puts it there is “The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan”, so it came from the other farm. Neither attorney is named anywhere in the passage, and the only thing to go on is which side each of them acts for. B offers the ordinary occasion of a boundary quarrel, a hedge nobody has kept, and the second sentence removes it: the bank was “cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other, and had stood since the enclosure”, and “both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839”, six years before the first letter and an unremarkable point in a laying cycle. Each wrong answer collides with a sentence instead of merely reaching past one.
